title: DOL Proposed Wage Hike for H-1B Workers Faces Legal Challenge Over Flawed Methodology
excerpt: A National Foundation for American Policy analysis argues the Department of Labor's proposed prevailing wage increases of up to 33% for H-1B visa holders are based on flawed data comparisons and could violate U.S. immigration law.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DOL's proposed wage rule could raise H-1B wages by 21% to 33% across all levels.
  • Critics argue the DOL's methodology creates a misleading wage gap for H-1B workers.
  • Independent studies show H-1B workers often earn equal to or more than U.S. counterparts.
  • The proposed rule may disqualify over 80% of current H-1B wage offers, impacting many workers.

  • The DOL's March 2026 proposed rule would raise required prevailing wages for H-1B workers by 21% to 33% across all four wage levels, shifting entry-level benchmarks from the 17th to the 34th percentile.
  • NFAP argues the rule compares early-career H-1B applicants against all workers in the same occupation — including senior professionals — creating a misleading wage gap that does not actually exist.
  • Multiple independent studies, including research by George Mason University and Glassdoor, have found H-1B workers are paid at or above the level of comparable U.S. workers.
  • The Cato Institute's analysis found the rule would disqualify over 80% of current H-1B wage offers, including most at the highest skill level, and could force hundreds of thousands of existing H-1B workers out of the country.

The Proposed Rule

The U.S. Department of Labor published a proposed rule in March 2026 that would sharply raise the minimum wages employers must pay H-1B visa holders and workers seeking employment-based green cards. Under the current four-tiered prevailing wage structure, Level I wages are pegged at the 17th percentile for a given occupation and geographic area. The proposed rule would raise that threshold to the 34th percentile — a 33% increase. Level II wages would jump from the 34th to the 52nd percentile, Level III from the 50th to the 70th, and Level IV from the 67th to the 88th percentile.

In dollar terms, the impact is substantial. According to DOL estimates, the average H-1B prevailing wage would increase by roughly $26,000 annually. In high-cost markets, the numbers are even steeper: a San Francisco employer hiring an entry-level software developer would see the required wage rise from $135,699 to $181,009 — an increase of more than $45,000. At the senior level, the required wage would jump from $213,512 to $259,801.

The DOL said it identified wage disparities between foreign national workers and similarly situated U.S. workers, claiming H-1B workers are paid approximately $10,000 less on average. The rule responds to a September 2025 Presidential Proclamation that directed the agency to review and revise H-1B wage levels.

Why Critics Say the Rule Is Likely Illegal

The National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP), a nonpartisan public policy research organization, released an analysis arguing the proposed rule is likely unlawful. NFAP's central argument is that the DOL's methodology compares mostly early-career H-1B professionals with all workers in the same occupations — including employees with significantly greater experience, longer job tenure, bonuses, and second-job income.

"The wage measures are not comparable, and the workers are not comparable. DOL has invented a gap and then selected percentiles to eliminate the average gap."

- Mark Regets, Labor Economist and Senior Fellow, NFAP

NFAP argued that Congress never intended employers to pay a wage premium for foreign nationals beyond market salaries, and that the proposed methodology "prices high-skilled foreign nationals out of the U.S. labour market." The organization pointed to the Supreme Court's June 2024 ruling in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which held that courts may not defer to an agency's interpretation of law simply because a statute is ambiguous — a standard that could make the rule more vulnerable to legal challenge.

The Cato Institute's analysis was even more pointed. Using American Community Survey data, Cato found that entry-level H-1B eligible workers earn wages at approximately the 19th percentile — closely matching the current 17th percentile benchmark. The proposed 34th percentile threshold bears no relationship to what actual entry-level workers earn, Cato argued. The think tank estimated the rule would disqualify more than 80% of current H-1B wage offers, including the majority at the highest skill level.

Data Contradicts DOL's Wage Gap Claim

Multiple independent studies suggest the DOL's central claim — that H-1B workers are underpaid relative to comparable U.S. workers — does not hold up. A study by George Mason University economist Michael Clemens found H-1B visa holders earned salaries up to 6% higher than comparable U.S. workers. Glassdoor research found H-1B salaries were roughly 2.8% higher across 10 cities and approximately 100 occupations. The Government Accountability Office found that H-1B electrical and electronics engineers earned median salaries about $5,000 higher than comparable U.S. engineers in the 20-39 age group.

NFAP also compared existing DOL prevailing wages against private wage surveys from Willis Towers Watson, finding only a 1% average difference across 55 city-occupation combinations in major metropolitan areas. Cato noted that DOL's own data show H-1B workers already receive wages averaging $10,191 above the current prevailing wage — evidence, the institute argued, that market forces are working as intended.

Impact on Indian Professionals

Indian nationals receive approximately 70% of all approved H-1B petitions, making the proposed rule especially consequential for the Indian diaspora. The wage increases, combined with the Trump administration's recently introduced $100,000 fee on new H-1B visa holders and a weighted lottery system that favors higher-wage applicants, represent a multi-front tightening of the H-1B pathway.

The KPMG analysis noted the proposed changes would affect not only H-1B filings but also PERM labor certification — the process through which employers sponsor workers for employment-based green cards. Higher prevailing wages in the PERM process could increase the overall cost of EB-2 and EB-3 sponsorship, potentially lengthening an already years-long wait for Indian professionals in the green card backlog.

What Comes Next

The public comment period on the proposed rule closed on May 26, 2026. A final version could take effect before the March 2027 H-1B electronic registration cycle. Immigration attorneys have indicated that legal challenges are not ruled out, particularly given the Loper Bright precedent limiting agency deference. The rule mirrors a similar Trump administration proposal from January 2021 that was struck down by federal courts in Washington and California for failing to follow proper notice-and-comment procedures. Whether the current version survives legal scrutiny may depend on whether courts find the DOL's statistical methodology meets the "reasoned analysis" standard the Administrative Procedure Act demands.
